strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in the T2V evaluation literature: existing benchmarks mostly target short, simple-prompt video generation, while this work targets long-form generation under complex, realistic prompts derived from real YouTube videos, with prompts that are substantially longer and scored as more complex than prior benchmarks (Table 1).

The evaluation suite is unusually comprehensive, spanning five major dimensions (static quality, text-video alignment, temporal quality, content clarity, HERD) decomposed into 26 sub-dimensions, including thoughtful new formulations such as event-level alignment via Hungarian matching with an order-inversion penalty (Eq. 1), and separate intra-/inter-event subject and background consistency to disentangle short- vs. long-range temporal coherence.

The paper goes beyond simply proposing metrics and includes several useful robustness/diagnostic analyses: checking whether static-quality bias contaminates other dimensions (Fig. 3, Table 5), examining entanglement between event-level alignment and temporal consistency, and studying how prompt complexity (semantic/structural/control) and content theme affect scores.

Evaluation of nine diverse open-source LVG baselines (diffusion-based, training-free, autoregressive, agent/multi-stage pipelines) provides a reasonably broad empirical picture, and the reported findings (strong static/short-term quality but weak inter-event coherence, fine-grained alignment, and narrative/thematic adherence) are plausible and actionable for the field.

Extensive appendices document prompt templates, metric implementations (e.g., transition smoothness formulation, event-level consistency math), baseline descriptions, and case studies, which aids methodological transparency.
weaknesses: The benchmark's central claims of validity rest almost entirely on MLLM/LLM judgments (Qwen2.5-VL, Seed1.5-VL, DeepSeek-V3.1) for alignment, content clarity, human action detection, and especially HERD (explicitly framed as capturing "human expectations"), yet the paper reports no human study or human-agreement/correlation analysis to validate that these automated judgments actually track human judgments. This is a significant soundness gap, particularly since prior benchmarks (e.g., VBench, EvalCrafter) that the paper builds on and compares against typically include such human-correlation validation.

HERD's pipeline is fully automated end-to-end: an MLLM evaluates real videos on abstract dimensions, an LLM turns those evaluations into yes/no questions, another LLM annotates question polarity, and a final MLLM answers the questions on generated videos — a long chain of LLM-generated/LLM-judged content with no independent human check on question quality, polarity accuracy, or answer correctness, raising concerns about circularity and compounding errors.

The prompt suite complexity comparison in Table 1 is scored by DeepSeek-V3.1, the same family of LLM used elsewhere in the pipeline, which is somewhat self-referential; a human-based or independent complexity assessment would strengthen this comparison claim.

Several fine-grained metrics (transition smoothness, event-level temporal consistency) depend on chained off-the-shelf tools (PySceneDetect, Grounded-SAM-2, RAFT, Time-R1) whose individual error rates and propagation through the pipeline are not analyzed, making it unclear how much noise these introduce into headline results.

Reproducibility is limited at submission time: code and full benchmark artifacts are not yet released (only a draft JSON of prompts), with the authors stating the full release will occur later after "code reorganization," which limits independent verification of the many custom evaluation components.

The benchmark evaluates only open-source baselines; none of the leading closed/commercial systems mentioned in the introduction (Sora, Veo, Kling, Runway Gen-4) are included, which somewhat limits the demonstrated discriminative power of the benchmark on today's strongest models.

With 240 total prompts spread across 18 themes (~13 per theme), sub-group analyses (e.g., theme-based breakdowns in Fig. 8/Table 6) may have limited statistical power, and no confidence intervals or variance estimates are reported for the main comparative results.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: most existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, etc.) use short, simple prompts and low-level metrics, while LoCoT2V-Bench targets long-form generation with complex, realistic prompts derived from real YouTube videos.

The evaluation suite is unusually comprehensive, spanning 5 major dimensions and 26 sub-dimensions, including novel higher-level constructs such as event-level alignment (with Hungarian matching and order-inversion penalties), intra-/inter-event temporal consistency, and the Human Expectation Realization Degree (HERD) metric targeting narrative/emotional qualities rarely assessed elsewhere.

Table 1 shows the constructed prompts are measurably longer and more complex (semantic/structural/control) than prompts in prior benchmarks, supporting the claim of a more challenging and realistic test suite.

Extensive secondary analyses are provided: checking whether static-quality scores bias other dimensions (Fig. 3, Table 5), examining metric entanglement between event-alignment and temporal consistency, and studying how prompt complexity and content theme affect scores — these lend some credibility to the robustness of the benchmark design.

Very thorough documentation in the appendix (full prompt templates, formulas for every sub-metric, case studies with qualitative examples), which aids understanding of the pipeline even though code is not yet released.
weaknesses: Core soundness gap: nearly all headline metrics (overall/event-level alignment, content clarity, HERD, human-action detection) rely entirely on MLLM/LLM judges (Qwen2.5-VL, Seed1.5-VL, DeepSeek-V3.1) with no reported correlation/agreement study against human annotators. For a benchmark whose central selling point is faithfully capturing "Human Expectation Realization," the complete absence of a human-agreement validation study is a serious unaddressed threat to the paper's central claims.

The chosen baselines (FreeNoise, MEVG, FreeLong, FIFO-Diffusion, DiTCtrl, CausVid, SkyReels-V2, Vlogger, VGoT) are mostly older, training-free, or less competitive open methods; none of the leading recent long/general video systems mentioned in the intro (Wan, HunyuanVideo, Sora/Veo/Kling/Runway-class models) are evaluated, even though some open-source strong systems were available, limiting the significance of the empirical findings about "current methods."

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code and full evaluation pipeline are not released ("will release... after code reorganization"), and the evaluation pipeline chains many separate tools (Grounded-SAM-2, Time-R1, PySceneDetect, multiple LLMs/MLLMs) without any error analysis of how compounding errors in this pipeline affect final scores.

Several design choices are introduced somewhat ad hoc without strong justification or ablation, e.g., the Relative Reference Upper Bound for aesthetic normalization derived from a specific external dataset, or the particular weighting/formulas for transition smoothness and event-level alignment (Eq. 1), raising concerns about sensitivity of results to these hyperparameter choices.
Modest benchmark scale (240 videos across 18 themes, ~13 samples/theme) limits the statistical reliability of the per-theme and complexity-stratified analyses presented in Sections 4.2 and 4.5.

No variance/error bars or significance testing are reported despite using repeated MLLM trials (mean-of-score) for content clarity and HERD, making it hard to judge how much metric noise affects the reported rankings.

The entanglement analysis between event-level alignment and temporal consistency (Section 4.4) identifies a potential confound in the metric design but does not resolve or correct for it, leaving an acknowledged validity issue unaddressed.
Presentation issues: dense tables, radar/violin plots with many overlapping curves are difficult to read, and some abbreviations (e.g., ITAE/ITRE) are inconsistently used across tables.

strengths: Addresses a clear and timely gap: existing T2V benchmarks mostly target short clips with simple prompts, while LoCoT2V-Bench is explicitly designed for long-form generation under complex, realistic prompts (Table 1 shows substantially longer and more complex prompts than prior work).

The evaluation suite is genuinely multi-dimensional and fine-grained (5 major dimensions, 26 sub-dimensions), going beyond conventional visual-fidelity/temporal-consistency metrics to include event-level alignment (via bipartite matching + temporal-order penalty), intra-/inter-event consistency, transition smoothness, content clarity, and a novel Human Expectation Realization Degree (HERD) metric for narrative/emotional/thematic qualities that prior benchmarks largely ignore.

Prompts are grounded in real-world collected YouTube videos across 18 themes rather than hand-crafted or templated text, improving ecological validity; the self-refine pipeline and manual factual checks add quality control.

Extensive empirical analysis beyond just leaderboard numbers: correlation analysis to check static-quality bias (Fig. 3, Table 5), entanglement analysis between event alignment and temporal consistency, robustness checks across theme categories, and prompt-complexity sensitivity analysis (Fig. 9) — these analyses strengthen the credibility and interpretability of the benchmark design.
Detailed appendix with full prompt templates, mathematical formulations for each sub-metric, and illustrative qualitative case studies, which aids understanding and partial reproducibility.
Reasonable ethical statement covering data collection compliance and content filtering.
weaknesses: No human evaluation or human-agreement study is reported to validate the many MLLM-based automatic metrics (text-video alignment, event-level alignment, content clarity, HERD). Since the paper's central claim is that this benchmark provides a more 'reliable' and human-aligned evaluation than prior CLIP-based approaches, the absence of correlation analysis between the proposed automated scores and human judgments is a significant soundness gap.

The nine baselines evaluated are mostly training-free extension techniques or older academic LVG methods (FreeNoise, MEVG, FreeLong, FIFO-Diffusion, DiTCtrl, CausVid, SkyReels-V2, Vlogger, VGoT); none of the frontier commercial/open systems mentioned in the introduction (Sora, Kling, Veo, Wan, Hunyuan) are benchmarked, which limits the demonstrated relevance of the benchmark for evaluating current state-of-the-art long video generators.

Reproducibility is only partial at submission time: the reproducibility statement indicates code and full benchmark release are pending ('will release ... after code reorganization'), so the complete evaluation pipeline cannot currently be verified by reviewers or the community.

Some design choices lack sensitivity/ablation analysis, e.g., the transition-smoothness normalization constants (b, c in Eq. 4), the choice of weighting across four similarity features (α1–α4), and the dependency of several metrics on a single MLLM backbone (Qwen2.5-VL / Seed1.5-VL / DeepSeek-V3.1) without testing robustness to backbone choice.

The prompt-complexity scoring itself is produced by an LLM (DeepSeek-V3.1) with few-shot examples, which is a somewhat circular self-assessment of benchmark difficulty rather than an independent or human-verified measure.

The heavy multi-tool evaluation pipeline (multiple MLLMs, Grounded-SAM-2, RAFT optical flow, PySceneDetect, DOVER++) raises practical concerns about computational cost and ease of adoption by the community, which is not discussed.

strengths: The benchmark construction is thorough and well-motivated: 234 real-world videos across 18 themes are converted into markedly longer and more complex multi-scene prompts (avg. 248.85 words, complexity 8.70) than prior benchmarks (Table 1, Fig. 5), addressing a genuine gap in evaluating long-form, complex text-to-video generation.

LoCoT2V-Eval is a genuinely multi-dimensional framework spanning perceptual quality, coarse-to-fine text-video alignment (with a novel hierarchical, gated VQA tree structure for fine-grained scene/character/background/camera verification), temporal quality (character/background consistency, warping error), dynamic quality (frame/segment/video-level), and a new HERD metric for higher-level narrative/emotional aspects via a decoupled Auditor-Evaluator design.

Extensive empirical study: 13 representative LVG methods spanning multi-prompt and direct-input paradigms are benchmarked, revealing a clear and interpretable capability gap (strong perceptual quality/background consistency vs. weak character consistency and fine-grained alignment), which is a useful diagnostic contribution to the field.

Reasonably careful validation efforts: human-annotated alignment analysis (PLCC/SRCC/KRCC) across nearly all sub-dimensions, an ablation on background-consistency computation (character removal vs. full frame), and a comparison of three alternative HERD scoring strategies (dual-agent vs QA-based vs direct scoring) which support specific design choices.

The appendix is unusually detailed and transparent, providing full prompt templates, baseline implementation details, per-sub-dimension results, category-level breakdowns, and case studies, which aids reproducibility and understanding of the pipeline despite its complexity.
weaknesses: Human alignment correlations for several key sub-dimensions are only moderate (e.g., Character Consistency PLCC 47.17/SRCC 49.90, Character Development PLCC 42.70, Visual Style PLCC 43.27, Narrative Flow PLCC 48.78), which weakens the claim that the framework reliably captures human judgment for exactly the dimensions (character consistency, narrative/character-level HERD) that the paper highlights as most diagnostic.

The human study underlying these correlations is small (5% of generated videos, 3 annotators), and the pre-fitted linear model used to aggregate Dynamic Quality sub-scores is fit on only 100 human-annotated videos, raising concerns about overfitting/generalizability of the aggregation weights.

Heavy reliance on closed-source, frequently-updated proprietary models (GPT-5, and various MLLMs) for prompt construction, complexity scoring, fine-grained VQA, and HERD evaluation creates reproducibility and cost concerns, since scores may drift as these APIs change or become unavailable, and independent verification/re-scoring is expensive.

The prompt "complexity" metric is scored by an LLM (DeepSeek-V3.2) against dimensions the authors themselves define, which is somewhat self-referential; moreover, Appendix C.4 shows only weak (and inconsistent-sign at times) correlation between this complexity score and actual model performance, calling into question how much diagnostic value the complexity axis adds beyond prompt length.

Baseline generation settings are not fully standardized (SkyReels-V2, Vlogger, VGoT use non-480p default settings while others use 480p), which could introduce confounds when comparing perceptual quality and other resolution-sensitive metrics across methods.

The main results table lacks any variance/uncertainty reporting (e.g., across seeds or repeated generations), making it hard to assess whether observed differences between top methods (e.g., LongLive vs. LongSANA) are robust rather than noise from a single seeded run per prompt.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: most existing T2V benchmarks (EvalCrafter, VBench, VBench2.0, VMBench) target short clips and relatively simple single-scene prompts, while LoCoT2V-Bench focuses on long-form, multi-scene, complex prompts built from real collected videos with hierarchical metadata (characters, backgrounds, camera motion).

The evaluation suite is comprehensive, covering perceptual quality, coarse-to-fine text-video alignment, temporal consistency (character/background/warping), multi-scale dynamic quality, and a novel HERD metric for narrative/emotional expectations.

Substantial engineering effort: a hierarchical, gated multi-turn VQA scheme for fine-grained alignment, SAM3+MLLM-verified character tracking for consistency, streaming adaptations of VBench/DEVIL/EvalCrafter metrics for long videos.
Useful ablations that strengthen some design choices, e.g. comparing BC with/without character masking and comparing the dual-agent HERD framework against QA-based and direct-scoring alternatives.
Reasonably broad empirical study across 13 representative LVG methods (multi-prompt and direct-input paradigms), with category-level breakdowns and complexity-vs-performance correlation analysis.
Extensive appendix with prompts, pipeline diagrams, and implementation details, which aids transparency about how scores are computed.
weaknesses: The central claim that LoCoT2V-Eval 'aligns well with human preferences' is only moderately supported: PLCC/SRCC for several core sub-dimensions are weak-to-moderate (e.g., Fine-grained Alignment ~53-54%, Character Consistency ~47-50%, most HERD sub-dimensions in the low-to-mid 40s%), which is concerning precisely for the dimensions the paper emphasizes as its main contribution (fine-grained alignment, character consistency, HERD).

The human-alignment study is very small in scale: only 5% of generated videos, scored by just 3 annotators, which limits the statistical reliability of the reported correlations and the generalizability of the 'validated human alignment' claim.

The benchmark/metric pipeline depends heavily on closed-source, versioned LLMs/MLLMs (GPT-5, proprietary models) for prompt construction, question generation, auditor/evaluator scoring, and even for defining 'complexity' itself. This raises reproducibility concerns, since these models are not fixed artifacts and results may not be stable across API versions or inaccessible to other labs without comparable API budgets.

The prompt 'complexity' metric used to argue superiority over prior benchmarks is itself computed by an LLM (DeepSeek-V3.2) scoring prompts against ill-defined rubrics, with no human validation of these complexity scores — this is somewhat circular evidence for the paper's main differentiator vs. prior benchmarks.

The correlation analysis between complexity metrics and model performance (Fig. 11) shows only weak negative correlations, undermining confidence that the carefully engineered 'complexity' axis is actually a meaningful discriminator of model capability, and the explanation (limited variance) is somewhat ad hoc.

Fairness of baseline comparison is questionable: generation settings are not fully standardized (some methods use default/non-480p settings), and StoryAdapter (an image-generation method) is paired with an external I2V model (Wan2.2) to produce video, introducing a confound not present for end-to-end video methods, which complicates direct comparison in Table 2.

The overall evaluation pipeline is extremely complex (multi-turn gated VQA trees, dual-agent HERD, SAM3+CLIP tracking, streaming variants of multiple sub-metrics, a separately pre-fit linear aggregation model for Dynamic Quality), which increases the risk of compounding errors across stages and makes independent auditing or reproduction by other groups difficult; important calibration details (e.g., the pre-fit DQ linear model weights) are not disclosed in the main text.
No discussion of the computational/API cost of running the full evaluation suite per video, which is an important practical consideration for a benchmark intended for broad community adoption.

Some reported findings (e.g., 'TVA correlates more with TQ and HERD', 'PQ correlates with DQ/TQ/HERD') are descriptive observations without statistical significance testing or deeper causal analysis, limiting their diagnostic value beyond face-value correlation numbers.

The dataset scale (234 videos, 18 themes) is modest relative to the scope of claims made about comprehensive, diagnostic benchmarking of 13 methods across 25 sub-dimensions, raising concerns about statistical power, especially for category-level breakdowns with imbalanced sample counts.

strengths: Addresses a clear gap: existing T2V benchmarks mostly target short, single-scene videos, while this work targets long-form, multi-scene, complex-prompt generation with real-world sourced videos (234 videos, 18 themes), producing substantially longer and more complex prompts than prior benchmarks (Table 1, Fig. 5), with hierarchical, scene-level metadata (characters, backgrounds, camera motion).

The LoCoT2V-Eval framework is unusually comprehensive, spanning perceptual quality, coarse-to-fine text-video alignment (including a novel hierarchical, gated multi-turn VQA scheme that penalizes hallucinated/missing scenes), temporal quality (character/background consistency, warping error), dynamic quality (frame/segment/video-level), and a new HERD metric for narrative/emotional fulfillment via a decoupled Auditor-Evaluator dual-agent design.

Extensive empirical validation effort: correlation analysis between dimensions, human-alignment studies (PLCC/SRCC/KRCC) across nearly all sub-dimensions, ablations comparing HERD design choices (dual-agent vs QA-based vs direct scoring) and background-consistency design choices (with vs without character masking), and category-level/complexity-level breakdowns.

Strong reproducibility effort relative to typical benchmark papers: full prompt templates, pipeline diagrams, baseline implementation details, generation settings, and annotation interface are provided in the appendix.

Benchmarks 13 diverse, recent LVG methods (both multi-prompt and direct-input paradigms) and surfaces clear, interpretable findings (e.g., large gap between background consistency and character consistency, and between overall and fine-grained alignment), which is genuinely useful diagnostic information for the field.
weaknesses: The entire evaluation pipeline is heavily dependent on proprietary, closed models (GPT-5, strong MLLMs) for prompt construction, scoring (OA, FGA, HERD), and even complexity scoring (DeepSeek-V3.2 self-assessing prompt complexity). This raises reproducibility concerns (model versions/behavior can change or be deprecated) and potential circularity (using an LLM to judge the complexity of LLM-generated prompts), as well as nontrivial cost/accessibility barriers for other researchers wishing to use the benchmark.

Human alignment evidence, while present, is only moderate for many sub-dimensions (e.g., Character Consistency PLCC 47%, Character Development PLCC ~42-43%, Visual Style ~43%), and is based on only 5% of generated videos with three annotators; inter-annotator agreement is not reported, making it hard to judge how much of the moderate correlation reflects noisy human labels versus real metric weaknesses.

The Dynamic Quality aggregation relies on a linear model fit to only 100 human-annotated videos, and this single fitted model is then used for all subsequent evaluation across 13 methods and hundreds of generated videos; no discussion of overfitting risk, confidence intervals, or sensitivity to the fitting sample is given.

The complexity metric analysis in the appendix itself shows the derived complexity scores have very low variance across the benchmark's own categories (2.8-4.4%), undermining the claimed discriminative power of the "complexity" axis and the correlation analysis between complexity and model performance (Fig. 11), which the authors acknowledge yields only weak (near-zero) correlations.

Generation settings are not fully uniform across baselines (several methods use non-480p defaults due to instability), and all results use a single fixed seed (seed=0) with no repeated-run variance reported, limiting confidence in the precision of the reported rankings, especially for closely-scored methods.

The benchmark construction pipeline (raw description -> story expansion -> post-processing) depends on substantial manual human verification at multiple stages, which is not quantified (e.g., no inter-rater reliability, no estimate of annotator time/cost), making it unclear how reproducible or scalable the benchmark curation process is for future extensions.
